PHSCS 587

Equilibrium carrier populations

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how donor doping shifts the equilibrium carrier populations and Fermi level

Conduction electrons and holes are mobile carriers with charges −q and +q. In an intrinsic semiconductor at thermal equilibrium, their concentrations are equal: n = p = nᵢ. The intrinsic concentration depends strongly on temperature.

In the nondegenerate equilibrium model, np = nᵢ². Fully ionized donor doping with ND much larger than nᵢ gives approximately n = ND and p = nᵢ²/ND when acceptor compensation is negligible. Ionized donors supply positive fixed charge that balances the mobile electrons in a neutral bulk region.

The Fermi level describes equilibrium occupancy. Moving it closer to the conduction-band edge increases electron population relative to holes. These simple concentration formulas require their stated temperature, ionization, and nondegeneracy assumptions; heavy doping or nonequilibrium needs a fuller model.

Example

Using the illustrative values nᵢ = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ and ND = 2 × 10¹⁵ cm⁻³, the approximation gives n ≈ 2 × 10¹⁵ cm⁻³ and p ≈ 5 × 10⁴ cm⁻³. Concentrations are numbers per volume, not net charge densities.

Sources and scope
  • MIT 6.012: Introduction to Semiconductors, Fall 2009
  • MIT 6.012: Thermal equilibrium and doping, Spring 2009

Practice

1. At fixed temperature within this approximation, what happens to majority and minority concentrations if ND increases tenfold?

Use n ≈ ND and p = nᵢ²/n.

Electron concentration rises approximately tenfold, while hole concentration falls to one tenth. Their equilibrium product stays nᵢ².

2. Why does donor doping fail to imply a negatively charged bulk material?

Count fixed ionized dopants as well as mobile carriers.

Donors leave positive ionized dopant charge while supplying mobile electrons. Bulk charge neutrality balances all fixed and mobile contributions; electron concentration alone does not give net charge.
